Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Including her could: - Show the foster child that she’s **seen and valued** (even temporarily). - Reinforce to your siblings that **family isn’t just blood**—it’s also about the people your mom loves and cares for. - Make the tradition more **meaningful for your mom**, who likely sees the foster child as part of her family. - **But:** If the foster child is uncomfortable or doesn’t want to be included, forcing her would be disrespectful. 3. **Why do you/your brother feel this way?** - **Lack of connection:** You haven’t spent much time with her, so she doesn’t "feel" like part of the family to you. That’s understandable—**traditions often rely on shared history**. - **Temporary nature:** The fear that she’ll leave soon makes it feel like a **one-time inclusion**, which might feel hollow. - **Siblings-only sentimentality:** The photos are a **private, inside-joke celebration** of your dynamic. To them, excluding her feels like **erasing her presence**. - **They want to include her** because it’s a way to **show appreciation for her** (e.g., "She’s been here for us, so we include her in our traditions"). - **They’re younger and may not understand** the emotional weight of traditions for older siblings. --- ### **Potential Solutions (Ranked by Compromise)** Here are ways to **honor your feelings while being fair to everyone**, depending on how much you’re willing to bend: #### **Option 1: Siblings-Only Photo + Separate Foster Child Photo** - **Take two photos:** 1. A **siblings-only** photo (your tradition, no foster child). 2. A **small group photo** of your mom with the foster child (or just the two of them) to acknowledge her. - **Why this works:** - Preserves your tradition *and* includes the foster child in a way that doesn’t feel forced. - Shows respect for her without making her feel like an afterthought. - Your mom gets **two photos to cherish** (one of her biological family, one of her foster family). #### **Option 2: Include Her, But Make It Clear It’s Temporary** - **Frame it as a "family + foster family" photo** and explain to your mom: > *"Mom, we wanted to include [foster child’s name] because she’s part of our family now, but we also wanted to keep our siblings-only tradition for you. So we’ll do both!"* - **Why this works:** - Validates your mom’s choice to foster while still honoring your tradition. - The foster child isn’t "erased"—she’s **acknowledged as part of the current family dynamic**. #### **Option 3: Let Her Opt Out (Respect Her Comfort)** - **Ask her directly** if she wants to be in the photo. If she says no, **don’t force it**. - **Why this works:** - Shows respect for her autonomy (some foster kids may feel awkward or self-conscious). - Avoids making her feel like a "project" or obligation. #### **Option 4: Modify the Tradition (If You’re Willing)** - **Make the tradition more inclusive** by: - Adding a **"family + friends/extended family"** photo *and* keeping the siblings-only one. - Including **past foster kids** (if applicable) to show continuity. - **Why this works:** - Signals that your family is **evolving** and open to new members. - But this might require **more emotional labor** from you and your brother. #### **Option 5: Do Nothing (But Prepare for Fallout)** - **Stick to siblings-only** and accept that your younger siblings might be upset. - **Why this might backfire:** - Your younger siblings could **feel excluded** from the tradition they’ve grown up with. - The foster child might **feel invisible**, which could affect her relationship with your family. - Your mom might **feel conflicted**—she loves the tradition but also loves the foster child. --- ### **Ethical Perspective: Are You Being an A-Hole?** - **If you exclude her without discussion:** **Yes, you’re being an asshole**—because: - You’re **ignoring her presence** in your home and your mom’s life. - You’re **prioritizing your comfort** over the feelings of your siblings and the foster child. - It sends the message that **she’s disposable** (which is cruel, even if unintentional). - **If you include her but make it clear it’s temporary:** **No, you’re not an asshole**—because: - You’re **compromising** while still honoring your tradition. - You’re **acknowledging her existence** without erasing your own feelings. - **If you let her opt out or take two photos:** **You’re being thoughtful and fair.** --- ### **Practical Steps to Resolve This** 1. **Talk to your siblings privately first.** - Say something like: > *"I know this tradition is important to you guys, and I don’t want to ruin it. But I also don’t want [foster child] to feel left out. What if we did [Option 1 or 2]?"* - Listen to their feelings—**they might have valid points**. 2. **Have a family meeting with your mom.** - Frame it as: > *"Mom, we love our tradition, but we also want to include [foster child] because she’s part of our family now. How do you feel about that?"* - Let your mom **guide the decision**—she knows the foster child best. 3. **Compromise on the photo.** - **Example:** - **Siblings-only photo** (your tradition). - **Mom + foster child photo** (to acknowledge her). - **Group photo of all of you** (if the foster child is comfortable). 4. **Prepare for pushback.** - Your younger siblings might **still be upset**, but **compromise is key in families**. - If they **refuse to compromise**, ask them: > *"Do you think this would hurt [foster child]’s feelings? Because that’s what matters most."* 5. **Reflect on your long-term feelings.** - If you **genuinely don’t want to include her**, ask yourself: - Will this feel wrong in 5 years when she’s gone? - Is there a way to **include her without losing the tradition’s meaning**? - If the answer is no, then **Option 1 or 2** is the way to go. --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** - **If you exclude her without discussion:** **Yes, you’re being an asshole** (even if unintentionally). - **If you include her but make it clear it’s temporary:** **No, you’re being reasonable.** - **If you let her opt out or take two photos:** **You’re handling it with maturity.** --- ### **What I’d Recommend** Given that this is a **throwaway post** (so you’re not seeking public judgment), I’d suggest: 1. **Take the middle ground:** Do **both photos** (siblings-only + mom + foster child). 2. **Explain to your siblings** that you’re trying to **honor everyone’s feelings**. 3. **Frame it as a growth opportunity:** This is a chance to **expand the tradition** to include more of your family. --- ### **Why This Matters** - **Foster kids often feel invisible.** Even if they’re in your home for months, they may not have **deep connections** with your siblings. Including them in traditions (when they’re comfortable) **shows them they belong**. - **Your mom will appreciate the effort.** She’s likely **proud of fostering** and would love to see the foster child included in her special day. - **Your siblings will respect you more** if you **compromise** instead of digging in your heels. --- ### **Bottom Line** You’re not **wrong** for feeling protective of your tradition, but **excluding her outright without discussion is selfish**. The best approach is to **find a middle ground** that honors your feelings while still being **kind and inclusive**.
